original.text: oṃ ity etad akṣaram idaṃ sarvaṃ tasyopavyākhyānaṃ bhūtaṃ bhavad bhaviṣyad iti sarvam oṅkāra eva | yac cānyat trikālātītaṃ tad apy oṅkāra eva
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: Om (oṃ) — this syllable (akṣara) is all this. Its explanation (upavyākhyāna) follows: what was, what is and what will be — all is just Oṃ; and whatever else lies beyond the three times is also just Oṃ.
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Opening (upakrama) of the text: the syllable is identified with all time and what is beyond time.

original.text: sarvaṃ hy etad brahmāyam ātmā brahma so 'yam ātmā catuṣpāt
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: For all this is brahman; this self (ātman) is brahman; and this same self has four quarters (catuṣpād).
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: The formula "ayam ātmā brahma" is stated here as the text's own thesis and the frame for the four quarters that follow.

original.text: jāgaritasthāno bahiḥprajñaḥ saptāṅga ekonaviṃśatimukhaḥ sthūlabhug vaiśvānaraḥ prathamaḥ pādaḥ
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: The first quarter (pāda) is the one common to all men (vaiśvānara): its station is waking (jāgarita-sthāna); it is outward-knowing (bahiḥprajña), has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and is the enjoyer of the gross (sthūlabhuj).
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: The seven limbs and nineteen mouths are not enumerated in this passage; the commentators supply lists (typically the seven cosmic limbs of Vaiśvānara, and five cognitive organs, five action organs, five vital breaths and four inner faculties). Not taken here as the plain sense of the text.

original.text: svaprasthāno 'ntaḥprajñaḥ saptāṅga ekonaviṃśatimukhaḥ praviviktabhuktaijaso dvitīyaḥ pādaḥ
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: The second quarter is the brilliant one (taijasa): its station is dream (svapna-sthāna); it is inward-knowing (antaḥprajña), has seven limbs and nineteen mouths, and is the enjoyer of the subtle or "separated" (praviviktabhuj).
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: "praviviktabhuk" is read by commentators as enjoyer of what is subtle/apart from the outer; the passage itself gives only the word. Limbs and mouths as at MU 3.

original.text: yatra supto na kañcana kāmaṃ kāmayate na kañcana svapnaṃ paśyati tat suṣuptam | suṣuptasthāna ekībhūtaḥ prajñānaghana evāndamayo hy ānandabhukcetomukhaḥ prājñaḥ tṛtīyaḥ pādaḥ
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: Where one asleep desires no desire and sees no dream — that is deep sleep (suṣupta). The third quarter is the intelligent one (prājña): its station is deep sleep; it has become one (ekībhūta), is a mass of cognition (prajñānaghana), consists of bliss (ānandamaya), is an enjoyer of bliss (ānandabhuj), and has thought (ceto) as its mouth.
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: "cetomukha" (thought as mouth) is obscure; commentators take it as the doorway to the cognition of the other two states. Deep sleep is defined here by the absence of desire and dream.

original.text: eṣaḥ sarveśvara eṣa sarvajña eṣo 'ntaryāmy eṣa yoniḥ sarvasya prabhavāpyayau hi bhūtānām
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: This one is lord of all (sarveśvara), knower of all (sarvajña), inner controller (antaryāmin), and the source (yoni) of all; for it is the origin and the dissolution of beings.
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: The referent of "eṣaḥ" (this one) is not stated in the verse; the commentators take it to be the prājña of the previous section (as the state in which the world is merged and from which it emerges). The paraphrase keeps "this one".

original.text: nāntaḥprajñaṃ na bahiḥprajñaṃ nobhayataḥprajñaṃ na prajñānaghanaṃ na prajñaṃ nāprajñam | adṛṣṭam avyavahāryam agrāhyam alakṣaṇam acintyam avyapadeśyam ekātmapratyayasāraṃ prapañcopaśamaṃ śāntaṃ śivam advaitaṃ caturthaṃ manyante | sa ātmā sa vijñeyaḥ
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: Not knowing inward, not knowing outward, not knowing both ways, not a mass of cognition, not knowing, not unknowing; unseen, not to be dealt with (avyavahārya), ungraspable, without distinguishing mark, unthinkable, not to be designated, with the one-self-conviction as its essence (ekātmapratyayasāra), the stilling of the world (prapañcopaśama), peaceful, auspicious (śiva), non-dual (advaita) — this they consider the fourth (caturtha). It is the self; it is to be known.
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: The fourth is described only by negations (first the three kinds of prajñā and prajñānaghana, then unseen ... not to be designated) and by a few positive words (ekātmapratyayasāra, prapañcopaśama, śānta, śiva, advaita). Commentators divide on whether "ekātmapratyayasāra" means "known only as the one self" or "the essence of the conviction of the one self".

original.text: so 'yam ātmādhyakṣaram oṅkāraḥ | adhimātraṃ pādā mātrā mātrāśca pādā akāra ukāro makāra iti
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: This same self, with respect to the syllable, is Oṃ; with respect to the measures (mātrā), the quarters are the measures and the measures are the quarters: a, u and m.
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: "adhimātram" is construed by commentators as "with respect to the measures". The sense "quarters are measures and measures are quarters" states a correspondence of the three quarters with a, u, m; the fourth quarter has no measure (MU 12).

original.text: jāgaritasthāno vaiśvānaraḥ akāraḥ prathamā mātrāpterādimattvād vā | āpnoti ha vai sarvān kāmān ādiś ca bhavati ya evaṃ veda
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: The vaiśvānara, whose station is waking, is the letter a, the first measure — because of obtaining (āpti) or because of being first (ādimattva). One who knows this thus obtains all desires and becomes first.
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Two grounds for the identification are offered (obtaining, being first). The result promised (all desires; becoming first) is a stated fruit (phala) of the knowledge; whether it is taken as arthavāda is a question for the interpretation layer.

original.text: svapnasthānas taijasa ukāro dvitīyā mātrotkarṣād ubhayatvād vā | utkarṣati ha vai jñānasantatiṃ | samānaś ca bhavati | nāsyābrahmavit kule bhavati ya evaṃ veda
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: The taijasa, whose station is dream, is the letter u, the second measure — because of exaltation (utkarṣa) or because of being in-between (ubhayatva, "both-ness"). One who knows this thus raises the continuity of knowledge (jñānasantati), becomes equal (samāna), and no one ignorant of brahman (abrahmavit) is born in his family.
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: "ubhayatva" is read by commentators as standing between waking and deep sleep. The verb "utkarṣati" and the phrase "samānaś ca bhavati" are given a plain sense here; commentators explain "equal" as being regarded equally by friends and foes.

original.text: suṣuptasthānaḥ prājño makāraḥ tṛtīyā mātrā miter apīter vā | minoti ha vā idaṃ sarvam apītiś ca bhavati ya evaṃ veda
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: The prājña, whose station is deep sleep, is the letter m, the third measure — because of measuring (miti) or because of merging (apīti). One who knows this thus measures all this and becomes the merging-place (apīti) of it.
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: "minoti idaṃ sarvam apītiś ca bhavati" is terse; the paraphrase keeps the two words (measure, merge) without a commentator's gloss.

original.text: amātraś caturtho 'vyavahāryaḥ prapañcopaśamaḥ śivo 'dvaitaḥ | evam oṅkāra ātmaiva | saṃviśaty ātmanātmānaṃ ya evaṃ veda
original.licence: Root text public domain; GRETIL e-text CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 — quotations with attribution

paraphrase: The fourth is without measure (amātra), not to be dealt with (avyavahārya), the stilling of the world (prapañcopaśama), auspicious (śiva), non-dual (advaita). Thus Oṃ is just the self (ātman). One who knows thus enters the self by the self.
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own paraphrase made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Closing (upasaṃhāra): returns to the opening identification of Oṃ with the self (MU 1, 2, 8) and states the result of knowing as entering the self by the self.

paraphrase: Thesis of the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, decided from the six marks of purport. The text identifies Oṃ, all time, brahman and the self (MU 1, 2, 8, 12) and teaches that this self has four quarters: waking (vaiśvānara), dream (taijasa) and deep sleep (prājña), which are matched to the measures a, u, m, and a fourth (turīya) that is without measure and known only by negation and by the words "stilling of the world, auspicious, non-dual" (MU 7, 12). Opening and closing (upakrama-upasaṃhāra): the text begins with "Oṃ is all this" (MU 1) and ends with "Oṃ is just the self; one who knows thus enters the self by the self" (MU 12). Repetition (abhyāsa): the quarters/states and the phrase "ya evaṃ veda" are repeated for each measure (MU 9–11), and prapañcopaśama-śiva-advaita recurs at MU 7 and 12. Novelty (apūrvatā): the four-quarter scheme of the self, the fourth as the unspoken beyond the three states, and the quarter-measure correspondence are taught here without a stated earlier source in the text itself. Stated result (phala): obtaining all desires and becoming first (MU 9), raising the continuity of knowledge (MU 10), measuring all and becoming its merging (MU 11), and entering the self by the self (MU 12). Praise (arthavāda): the fruit-promises of MU 9–11 are in the form of praise of the knower; their weight is left to the interpretation layer. Reasoned demonstration (upapatti): the passages give brief grounds only for the a-u-m assignments (obtaining/being first; exaltation/in-between; measuring/merging, MU 9–11); the four quarters are otherwise stated, not argued. Main teaching: the self is one and non-dual; the three states are its quarters and the fourth is its own nature; Oṃ is the means of seeing this.
speaker: Upaniṣad (śruti; no named speaker)
translation_basis: own summary made directly from the Sanskrit text; no published translation consulted
notes: Marks assessed by the extractor from the twelve sections; the weighting of the fruit-promises as arthavāda is not decided here.
